title: Al-Malik, the King
hook: the King, whose kingdom never ends, and everything in your hands on loan from it
tomorrow: a King with no flaw at all. what does 'pure' even mean?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ar-Rahim: mercy close to each one, and family ties named from Allah's own name. Mercy for me. The rest of the week comes back in a moment.

The lease, the car title, the account in your name: paperwork says who owns what. Yesterday ended on a question: if mercy is that close, who's actually in charge here? The Qur'an answers with the third name. Al-Malik, the King. Surah al-Mulk opens, in Pickthall's words: Blessed is He in Whose hand is the Sovereignty.

Al-Malik comes from the root m-l-k: to own, to rule. Surah Al Imran gives a line to say about it, beginning, in Pickthall's words: Say: O Allah! Owner of Sovereignty! The verse goes on: You give sovereignty to whom You will, and You take it from whom You will. Every crown is on loan, and so is every key on your ring. In the Qur'an, Pharaoh is the king who forgot it, announcing to his people that he was their highest lord. That doesn't make things cheap. A borrowed thing is treated with more care, not less; it just isn't gripped. And that's this week, too, held in an open hand. The forty as a life. One, by heart. Pass one on. Every name a door. Mercy for all. Mercy for me. Six things gathered, none of them owned, all of them lent to carry. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Qur'an's word for a kingdom, mulk, comes from the same root as the word for owning.
screen: `M-L-K: TO OWN, TO RULE.` · `OWNER OF SOVEREIGNTY.` · `LENT, SO HELD WITH CARE.` · `SIX THINGS, ON LOAN.` · then, large: `HIS KINGDOM.`

segments.voice: Hold something you own on your open palm: keys, a ring, your phone. Don't grip it; let it rest there, flat. For the sit, keep the hand open, holding it the way you'd hold something lent.
Al-Malik: the King, the Owner of sovereignty, whose kingdom never ends.
Hold onto this: his kingdom, and everything in my hands on loan from it. That's a week of names begun.

howItsDone: At a loss, Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we belong to Allah and to Him we return, and many think of what they hold as a trust from Him.

fork.setup: a friend lends you her laptop for a week while yours is in the shop. it's older than yours and a bit slow. what does Al-Malik say about how you treat it?
options: with care; what's lent is handled carefully, never treated as yours.

fork.reveal: if everything is on loan, a borrowed thing gets more care, not less. that's how the name loosens the grip without making things cheap.
